title: Survey on Monocular Metric Depth Estimation
relevance_assessment: Highly relevant – the paper is a comprehensive survey of Monocular Metric Depth Estimation (MMDE) covering methods, datasets, recent advances (2023‑2025), performance benchmarks, and open challenges, directly addressing the requested topic.
key_findings: MMDE has progressed from geometry‑based pipelines to deep models that predict absolute scale, enabling deployment in SLAM, AR/VR, and autonomous driving.
Zero‑shot MMDE methods such as ZoeDepth (2023) and UniDepth (2024) achieve strong cross‑domain generalization by combining relative depth pre‑training with metric binning or camera‑invariant modules.
Adaptive binning strategies (AdaBins, LocalBins, BinsFormer) markedly improve accuracy by learning data‑dependent depth discretization.
Patch‑based and transformer‑based architectures (PatchFusion, PatchRefiner, BinsFormer) preserve fine‑grained structures but increase computational cost.
Generative diffusion models (Marigold, GeoWizard, DMD) can recover high‑frequency geometry, yet remain slower and mostly focused on relative depth.
Large‑scale semi‑supervised data (Depth Anything’s 62 M self‑annotated images) and synthetic‑real hybrid datasets are crucial for zero‑shot performance.
limitations: Generalization to unseen domains still limited; models suffer from geometric blurring and loss of detail in high‑resolution or out‑of‑distribution scenes.
Patch‑based methods improve detail but introduce latency that hinders real‑time use.
Diffusion‑based MMDE offers superior fidelity but is computationally intensive and often predicts only relative depth.
Lack of standardized evaluation protocols and inconsistent reporting of metric vs. relative depth impede fair comparison across works.
evidence_snippets: “Monocular Metric Depth Estimation (MMDE) overcomes this challenge by producing depth maps with absolute scale… this survey reviews the evolution of MMDE, from geometry‑based methods to state‑of‑the‑art deep models…”
“Zero‑shot MMDE was a breakthrough in ZoeDepth (Bhat et al., 2023), which extended MiDaS with adaptive metric binning and scene‑aware routing, achieving strong cross‑domain generalization…”
“AdaBins introduced dynamic depth bin allocation (Bhat et al., 2021), refined by LocalBins… while BinsFormer integrated Transformers for global‑local bin optimization (Li et al., 2024c).”

“Patch‑based methods improve detail by combining local and global cues. BoostingDepth and PatchFusion use multi‑resolution fusion… PatchRefiner introduces Detail and Scale Disentangling loss to sharpen boundaries…”

“Generative diffusion models… Marigold achieves sharper predictions in reflective and transparent regions (Ke et al., 2024), while GeoWizard introduces scene‑aware decoupling and normal map integration… DMD incorporates field‑of‑view conditioning and log‑scale parameterization for accurate zero‑shot MMDE (Saxena et al., 2023).”

“Depth Anything employs a semi‑supervised framework generating 62M self‑annotated images, enabling strong cross‑domain adaptation… Depth Anything V2 leverages synthetic supervision with pseudo‑labeling and gradient‑matching loss…”

“Challenges remain: models often suffer from geometric blurring, loss of fine details, and degraded performance in high‑resolution or cross‑domain scenarios… trade‑off between accuracy and efficiency (Spencer et al., 2024b).”
summary: The survey provides a thorough overview of Monocular Metric Depth Estimation (MMDE) up to 2025, tracing the shift from geometry‑based pipelines to deep networks that output absolute depth. It highlights key methodological trends: zero‑shot models (ZoeDepth, UniDepth) that blend relative pre‑training with metric binning; adaptive binning (AdaBins, LocalBins, BinsFormer) for finer discretization; transformer and patch‑based designs (PatchFusion, PatchRefiner) that improve boundary preservation at the cost of runtime; and generative diffusion approaches (Marigold, GeoWizard, DMD) offering high‑frequency detail but limited efficiency. Large‑scale semi‑supervised datasets and synthetic‑real hybrids are identified as pivotal for generalization. Despite advances, persistent issues include domain generalization, geometric blurring, and the lack of unified benchmarks, underscoring the need for more efficient, detail‑preserving, and universally evaluated MMDE solutions.

title: Deep Learning‑based Depth Estimation Methods from Monocular Image and Videos: A Comprehensive Survey
source: Full paper text provided in the prompt
relevance_assessment: Highly relevant. The survey reviews >160 papers up to early 2024, presents a detailed taxonomy (input/output modalities, network architectures, supervision levels, datasets, domain‑adaptation), discusses recent trends such as vision‑transformers, attention mechanisms, self‑supervised video training, and outlines future research gaps that match the 2023‑2025 focus.
key_findings: A unified taxonomy that classifies monocular depth methods by input type (single image vs video), architecture (CNN, ViT, RNN, GAN, hybrid), supervision (3‑D supervised, self‑supervised, semi‑/weakly‑supervised, online) and domain‑adaptation strategies.
Identification of core challenges: depth ambiguity, lack of camera parameters, brightness inconsistency, temporal consistency, moving objects, and the difficulty of obtaining dense ground‑truth.
Self‑supervised training is now the dominant paradigm, using image reprojection losses, photometric consistency, and masking strategies to handle occlusions and dynamic scenes.
Attention mechanisms (spatial, channel‑wise, hybrid) and multi‑scale feature fusion markedly improve depth fidelity, especially at object boundaries.
Domain‑adaptation is tackled by fine‑tuning and data‑style transformation (GAN‑based). Emerging trends include shape‑biased Vision Transformers and CLIP‑based few‑shot depth estimation.
Open gaps: poor handling of thin/distant objects, dynamic/non‑rigid motions, reflective/transparent materials, aerial/panoramic viewpoints, real‑time constraints, and model explainability.
limitations: The survey stops at early‑2024 and does not cover the very latest transformer‑based models (e.g., DepthAnything 2024) or large‑scale foundation‑model approaches that emerged after its compilation.
Quantitative performance tables are absent; the paper focuses on qualitative taxonomy, limiting direct comparison of state‑of‑the‑art accuracies.
The 360° monocular depth literature is explicitly excluded, despite growing interest in omnidirectional depth estimation.
evidence_snippets: “We present a broad taxonomy … based on their input and output modalities, network architectures, and learning methods.”
“General challenges … 3D‑to‑2D mapping ambiguity, camera parameters estimation, brightness inconsistency … Temporal consistency and smoothness … Moving objects and moving camera.”

“Self‑supervised monocular depth estimation methods … formulate the problem as an image reprojection problem … minimize the dissimilarity … between the synthesized (reprojected) view and the target view.”
“Attention mechanisms focus on more important features … Spatial attention … Channel‑wise attention … Hybrid … improve depth estimation with respect to meaningful semantic information.”
“Domain adaptation … fine‑tuning … data transformation … GAN‑based style transfer … AdaDepth … to transform the style of synthetic data to match real data.”

“Inaccurate results for thin, small, and distant objects … Limitations in self‑supervision … Inaccurate depth for complex materials … Methods limited to estimate at eye‑level depth … Lack of explainability … Real‑time depth estimation … CLIP models for depth … human‑biased depth bins.”
summary: The survey delivers a comprehensive overview of monocular depth estimation up to early 2024, organizing more than 160 works into a detailed taxonomy that spans input modalities, network designs (CNN, Vision Transformer, RNN, GAN, and hybrids), and supervision schemes (fully supervised, self‑supervised, semi‑/weakly‑supervised, online). It highlights persistent challenges—depth ambiguity, camera pose uncertainty, illumination variance, and temporal consistency—while emphasizing the rise of self‑supervised video training and attention‑enhanced multi‑scale fusion. Domain‑adaptation methods, including fine‑tuning and GAN‑based style transfer, are surveyed, and emerging directions such as shape‑biased Transformers and CLIP‑driven few‑shot depth are noted. The paper also pinpoints gaps: poor handling of thin or reflective objects, dynamic scenes, aerial viewpoints, real‑time constraints, and model explainability, setting a clear agenda for research in 2023‑2025.

title: Towards Real-Time Monocular Depth Estimation for Robotics: A Survey
relevance_assessment: The paper is a comprehensive survey of monocular depth estimation (MDE) methods up to 2021, covering classic SfM, handcrafted-feature, and deep‑learning approaches, as well as datasets, metrics, and robotic applications. While it provides essential background for understanding the evolution of MDE, it does not include works published after 2021, so its direct relevance to the 2023‑2025 period is limited to historical context and identified future research directions.
key_findings: Classifies MDE methods into three categories: Structure‑from‑Motion (SfM), traditional handcrafted‑feature, and deep‑learning‑based (Section III‑V).
Summarizes 197 articles (1970‑2021) and highlights the rapid growth of publications after 2015 (Fig. 2).

Provides a detailed taxonomy of deep‑learning architectures (multi‑scale, encoder‑decoder, CNN‑CRF, GAN) and discusses real‑time lightweight models such as FastDepth and DepthNet Nano (Section V‑A‑4).

Analyzes performance on KITTI, showing supervised methods achieve the best accuracy, with Bhat et al. [71] achieving the lowest Abs Rel (0.058) but at high computational cost (Section VII‑A, Table IV).

Identifies major open challenges and future directions: richer diverse datasets, real‑time accuracy‑efficiency trade‑offs, domain adaptation, semi‑supervised learning, multimodal fusion, and interpretability (Conclusion).
limitations: Coverage ends in 2021; the survey does not discuss important MDE advances from 2022‑2025 such as transformer‑based depth networks, self‑supervised video‑centric methods, or recent large‑scale synthetic‑to‑real adaptation techniques.
Running‑time analysis is incomplete because many papers do not report inference speed, limiting direct comparison of real‑time suitability.
Depth‑completion methods are only briefly reviewed and lack systematic evaluation or integration with MDE pipelines.
evidence_snippets: “We classify the reviewed methods into three main categories: Structure from Motion (SfM)-based methods, traditional handcrafted feature‑based methods, and state‑of‑the‑art deep learning‑based methods.” (Section I)
“Figure 2 shows the number of published articles on MDE from 2000 to 2021… the overall development trend of MDE is to push the increase of accuracy.” (Section I)

Table IV presents a comparison of 42 representative methods on KITTI, highlighting that supervised methods achieve the best error/accuracy metrics and that Bhat et al. [71] obtains the lowest Abs Rel (0.058).

“Real‑time monocular depth estimation with accuracy and efficiency balance: … researchers have begun to develop real‑time MDE methods [27], [69], [113], [137]. However, the accuracy of these methods is inferior to state‑of‑the‑art methods.” (Conclusion)

Future‑direction list: “Collecting rich scene datasets… Real‑time monocular depth estimation with accuracy and efficiency balance… Monocular depth estimation with domain adaptation… Semi‑supervised monocular depth estimation… Depth estimation with information fusion… Interpretability of monocular depth estimation networks.” (Conclusion)
summary: This 2021 survey provides an extensive overview of monocular depth estimation up to the start of 2021, organizing methods into SfM, handcrafted and deep‑learning categories, and detailing datasets, metrics, and robotic applications. It reports that supervised deep models dominate performance, while recent lightweight networks aim for real‑time operation at some accuracy loss. The paper pinpoints key research gaps—insufficiently diverse datasets, the need for accuracy‑efficient real‑time models, domain adaptation, semi‑supervised learning, multimodal fusion, and model interpretability—offering a roadmap that aligns with many trends emerging in 2023‑2025. However, it does not cover the latest transformer‑based or video‑self‑supervised approaches that dominate the field after 2021, limiting its direct applicability to the current survey period.
